summary: Specifies a leasequery exchange for DHCPv6, so lease information about clients can be obtained from a server. It defines the data that can be retrieved and the behavior of requestors and servers. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A DHCPv6 server knows which addresses and prefixes it has handed out. This RFC adds a question and an answer to the DHCPv6 protocol, so that another device, such as a router at the edge of a broadband network, can ask the server what a particular client holds without changing anything.

questions: what is a dhcpv6 lease query by client id
what are dhcpv6 leasequery status codes
subtitle: A way for a device to ask a DHCPv6 server which addresses and prefixes a client holds.

tldr.problem: Devices such as an access concentrator at the edge of a broadband network need to know where a client is and what it holds, but DHCPv6 had no way to ask a server for that information programmatically.
tldr.mechanism: Two new DHCPv6 messages, LEASEQUERY and LEASEQUERY-REPLY, carry a query option that names the query type and a link address, and a reply that returns the client's data in a new client data option.
tldr.outcome: A requestor can look up a client by address or by client identifier. The query changes nothing on the server, and the RFC asks that the exchange be protected with the usual DHCPv6 security mechanisms.

facts.label: Client last transaction time option code

today: RFC 5007 is a Proposed Standard from September 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. IANA registered two new DHCPv6 message types, five new option codes, four new status codes and a new registry for the query-type codes, with QUERY_BY_ADDRESS set to 1 and QUERY_BY_CLIENTID set to 2.

sections.title: Why Query a DHCPv6 Server
sections.content:
DHCPv6 specifies a mechanism for assigning both IPv6 address and configuration information to IPv6 nodes, and the IPv6 prefix options for DHCPv6 specify a mechanism for the automated delegation of IPv6 prefixes. As with DHCPv4, DHCPv6 servers maintain authoritative information related to their operations, including lease information for IPv6 addresses and delegated prefixes.

The requirement exists in various types of IPv6 deployment, particularly broadband ones, to use DHCPv6 for retrieving data related to the operation of DHCPv6 servers programmatically. It is desirable to extract lease information about IPv6 addresses and delegated prefixes assigned using DHCPv6. One example where this information has value is in broadband networks, to facilitate access control by edge devices. This capability to extract lease data from a DHCPv6 server programmatically is called leasequery.

The capability described here parallels the DHCPv4 leasequery capability documented in RFC 4388, and shares its basic motivations, background, design goals and constraints. The differences are due to the differences between IPv4 and IPv6, and by extension between DHCPv4 and DHCPv6. For example, Neighbor Discovery is used in IPv6 instead of the Address Resolution Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A broadband provider hands out addresses with DHCPv6, and the router at the edge of its network needs to know where each customer is so it can forward their traffic and check that the traffic comes from the right place. Until now it could only learn that by watching DHCP messages go past. This RFC lets it ask the server directly.

sections.title: On-Demand and Anticipatory Queries
sections.content:
The LEASEQUERY message is a query message only. It does not affect the state of the IPv6 address or prefix, or the binding information associated with it.

The on-demand leasequery capability allows a requestor to ask for just the information needed to satisfy an immediate need. If the requestor is an access concentrator, the immediate need is typically that it has received an IPv6 packet and needs to refresh its information about the client to which that address is currently leased. The request is then by address, which fits the single request and response cycle common to other DHCPv6 message exchanges.

This approach has limitations when used with prefix delegation, because no traffic may arrive: the access concentrator may be unable to inject the appropriate routing information into the routing infrastructure, for example after a reboot. It does work if the access concentrator is configured to inject routing information for a prefix that aggregates potentially delegated prefixes, or if the access concentrator and the requesting router use a routing protocol, so that the requesting router can trigger the access concentrator to request the information and inject routing information into the routing infrastructure.

A second approach, the anticipatory query, would use a leasequery-like capability to rebuild an internal data store holding information available from a DHCPv6 server. The rebuilding could take place as soon as the need to rebuild it is discovered, such as on booting, rather than waiting for specific packets to trigger a piecemeal update, and it would remove the limitation described above for prefix delegation. This anticipatory query is not specified in this document and is an area of future work.
sections.plainLanguage: The query is meant to be asked when something needs to be known right now, for example when a packet arrives and the router must find out who it belongs to. Asking for the whole database at once would remove the problem of not having any traffic to trigger a query, but that approach is left as future work.

sections.title: The Two Messages and the Query Option
sections.content:
The LEASEQUERY and LEASEQUERY-REPLY messages use the client and server message formats described in the DHCPv6 specification, section 6. Two new message codes are defined. LEASEQUERY, code 14, is sent by a requestor to any available server to obtain information on a client's leases; the options in an OPTION_LQ_QUERY option determine the query. LEASEQUERY-REPLY, code 15, is sent by a server in response, containing client data.

The Query option, OPTION_LQ_QUERY with code 44, is used only in a LEASEQUERY message and identifies the query being performed. It holds a query type, a link address, and the options that provide the data needed for the query. Its length field is 17 plus the length of the query-options field. The link address is a global address the server uses to identify the link to which the query applies, or 0::0 if unspecified.

Two query types are defined. QUERY_BY_ADDRESS, value 1, requires an OPTION_IAADDR option, and returns only the information for the client that has a lease for the specified address or was delegated a prefix containing it, if that information is available. The link address, if it is not 0::0, names the link on which the client is located when the address in the OPTION_IAADDR option is of insufficient scope. QUERY_BY_CLIENTID, value 2, requires an OPTION_CLIENTID option, and returns the bindings for a specific client on a specific link, or a list of the links on which the client has one or more bindings. If the link address is 0::0, the server should search all of its links for the client.

The query options may also include an OPTION_ORO option to indicate the options for each client that the requestor would like returned. This OPTION_ORO is distinct from any OPTION_ORO in the requestor's LEASEQUERY message. If a server receives a query type it does not support, it should return an UnknownQueryType status code; if it receives a supported query type whose query options are missing a required option, it should return a MalformedQuery status code.
sections.plainLanguage: The question is a new message type carrying a new option. The option says which kind of question it is, which link it is about, and the address or the client identifier being asked about. The reply comes back with the answer.

sections.title: The Options a Reply Carries
sections.content:
The Client Data option, OPTION_CLIENT_DATA with code 45, encapsulates the data for a single client on a single link in a LEASEQUERY-REPLY message. Its length field is the length in octets of the encapsulated client-options field, and those encapsulated options include OPTION_CLIENTID, OPTION_IAADDR, OPTION_IAPREFIX and OPTION_CLT_TIME, together with other options specific to the client that the requestor asked for in the OPTION_ORO. The server must return all of the client's statefully assigned addresses and delegated prefixes with a non-zero valid lifetime on the link.

The Client Last Transaction Time option, OPTION_CLT_TIME with code 46, is encapsulated in an OPTION_CLIENT_DATA option and says how long ago the server last communicated with the client, in seconds. Its length is 4 and its value is a positive number of seconds since the server last communicated with the client on that link.

The Relay Data option, OPTION_LQ_RELAY_DATA with code 47, is used only in a LEASEQUERY-REPLY message and provides the relay agent information used when the client last communicated with the server. Its length is 16 plus the length of the DHCP-relay-message. The peer address is the address of the relay agent from which the relayed message was received, and the DHCP-relay-message is the last complete relayed message, excluding the client's message OPTION_RELAY_MSG, that the server received. The option must not be returned if the server does not have such information, and if returned the message must contain a valid, perhaps multi-hop, RELAY-FORW message with the innermost OPTION_RELAY_MSG removed. It should only be returned if the requestor asked for it in the OPTION_ORO.

The Client Link option, OPTION_LQ_CLIENT_LINK with code 48, is used only in a LEASEQUERY-REPLY message and identifies the links on which the client has one or more bindings. It is used in reply to a query when no link address was specified and the client is found to be on more than one link. Its length is the length of the list of links in octets and must be a multiple of 16. The requestor may then repeat the query once for each link address returned.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply carries one option per client, holding that client's identifier, its addresses and prefixes, and a timestamp. It can also carry the relay agent's address and the last message the relay forwarded, and a list of the links the client appears on.

sections.title: Status Codes and Message Validation
sections.content:
Four status codes are defined. UnknownQueryType, value 7, means the query type is unknown to or not supported by the server. MalformedQuery, value 8, means the query is not valid, for example because a required query option is missing. NotConfigured, value 9, means the server does not have the target address or link in its configuration. NotAllowed, value 10, means the server does not allow the requestor to issue this LEASEQUERY.

Servers must discard any received LEASEQUERY message that does not include an OPTION_CLIENTID option, that includes an OPTION_SERVERID option whose contents do not match the server's identifier, or that does not include an OPTION_LQ_QUERY option. Requestors and clients must discard any received LEASEQUERY message.

Requestors must discard any received LEASEQUERY-REPLY message that does not include an OPTION_SERVERID option, that does not include an OPTION_CLIENTID option or whose OPTION_CLIENTID contents do not match the DUID of the requestor, or whose transaction-id field does not match the value used in the original message. Servers and relay agents on the server port, 547, must discard any received LEASEQUERY-REPLY message.
sections.plainLanguage: Four error codes cover the ways a query can go wrong: an unknown question, a broken question, a link the server does not know, and a request the server refuses. Both sides also check that the message is addressed to them and matches the exchange they started, and drop it if not.

sections.title: What the Requestor Does
sections.content:
The requestor sets the message type field to LEASEQUERY and generates a transaction ID, which it puts in the transaction-id field. It must include an OPTION_CLIENTID option to identify itself to the server, and it must include an OPTION_LQ_QUERY option with the query type, link address and query options set to suit that query type. It should include an OPTION_SERVERID if it is not unicasting the LEASEQUERY but wants a response only from a specific server.

The requestor may be configured to use a list of destination addresses, which may include unicast addresses, the All_DHCP_Servers multicast address, or other addresses chosen by the network administrator. If it has not been configured, it may use the All_DHCP_Servers multicast address as the default. It should send LEASEQUERY to one or more DHCPv6 servers known to hold authoritative information about the query target; in the absence of such information it should send to all the servers it knows about.

The retransmission parameters are LQ_TIMEOUT as the initial timeout, 1 second; LQ_MAX_RT as the maximum timeout value, 10 seconds; LQ_MAX_RC as the maximum number of retry attempts, 5; and a maximum retransmission delay of 0. If the exchange fails, the requestor acts on its own local policy, for example selecting another server from its list, sending to multiple servers by multicasting to the All_DHCP_Servers address, or terminating the request.

A successful LEASEQUERY-REPLY is one without a status code option, or with a success code. There are three variants. If the server had bindings for the requested client, the message includes an OPTION_CLIENT_DATA option, and the requestor extracts the client data and updates its binding information database; if that option contains no OPTION_CLT_TIME, the requestor should silently discard the option. If the server found the client on multiple links, the message includes an OPTION_CLIENT_LINK option, and the requestor must issue further LEASEQUERY messages using each returned link address. If the server had no bindings for the client, neither option is present.

A requestor may receive lease data on the same client from several sources. If the data from two sources are of different types or values, they are disjoint, and the requestor should merge them. If they are of the same type and value, they are overlapping, and are also called conflicting data. The requestor should use the OPTION_CLT_TIME to resolve conflicts that came from different servers, and should accept the data with the most recent OPTION_CLT_TIME.
sections.plainLanguage: The requestor identifies itself, states its question, and waits. If the answer says the client is on several links, it asks again for each link in turn. If two servers give it different answers about the same client, it keeps the one with the more recent timestamp.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
Upon receipt of a valid LEASEQUERY message, the DHCPv6 server locates the requested client, collects data on the client, and constructs and returns a LEASEQUERY-REPLY. A LEASEQUERY message cannot be used to assign, release, or otherwise modify bindings or other configuration information. The server sets the message type field to LEASEQUERY-REPLY and copies the transaction ID from the LEASEQUERY message.

If the query type is not a known or supported value, the server adds a status code option with the UnknownQueryType code. If the query options do not contain the required options for the query type, it adds a status code option with the MalformedQuery code. A server may also restrict LEASEQUERY messages, or query types, to certain requestors, in which case it may discard the message or answer with the NotAllowed status code.

If the query specified a non-zero link address, the server must use it to find the appropriate link for the client. For a QUERY_BY_ADDRESS with a 0::0 link address, the server uses the address from the OPTION_IAADDR option to find the link. If the server cannot find the link, it should answer with the NotConfigured status. For a QUERY_BY_CLIENTID with a 0::0 link address, the server must search all of its links; if the client is on a single link, the server should return that client's data in an OPTION_CLIENT_DATA option, and if the client is on more than one link, it must return the list of links in the OPTION_CLIENT_LINK option and no client data.

An OPTION_CLIENT_DATA option must minimally contain OPTION_CLIENTID, OPTION_IAADDR and or OPTION_IAPREFIX, and OPTION_CLT_TIME. It should include the options requested in the OPTION_ORO that are acceptable to return. DHCPv6 servers should be configurable with a list of sensitive options that must not be returned to the requestor even when the requestor asks for them.
sections.plainLanguage: The server looks up the client, builds the answer and returns it, and the query changes nothing on the server. Some options can be marked sensitive so that they are never handed out, whatever the requestor asks for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Access concentrators are expected to be common leasequery requestors. An access concentrator that uses DHCPv6 gleaning, refreshed with LEASEQUERY messages, will maintain accurate client and binding information. This ensures that it can forward data traffic to the intended destination in the broadband access network, can perform IPv6 source address verification of datagrams from the access network, and can encrypt traffic that can only be decrypted by the intended access modem. The leasequery capability therefore allows an access concentrator to provide considerably enhanced security.

The DHCPv6 security considerations detail the general threats to DHCPv6, and thus to LEASEQUERY messages, and describe securing communication between relay agents and servers as well as clients and servers. If the requestor is an access concentrator, the IPsec-based security described in section 21.1 of the DHCPv6 specification should be used. Other requestors are essentially DHCPv6 clients, so DHCPv6 authentication is an appropriate mechanism for securing LEASEQUERY and LEASEQUERY-REPLY messages. The number of leasequery requestors and servers in an administrative domain is relatively small, so shared key distribution issues are minimized. Once these approaches are in place, the DHCPv6 server should only be communicating with trusted leasequery requestors.

Not all traffic originates directly from these trusted requestors. Trusted relay agents can relay LEASEQUERY messages from untrusted requestors, and this should be prevented at least at the perimeter relay agents, or on all relay agents unless relayed LEASEQUERY messages are required. DHCPv6 servers may be configured to discard relayed LEASEQUERY messages or restrict relay chaining.

Even trusted access concentrators may generate LEASEQUERY requests as a result of activity external to the access concentrator, so they should minimise the risk of denial-of-service attacks on the DHCPv6 servers by minimising the generation of LEASEQUERY messages. They should employ negative caching, caching the fact that a recent query failed to return client data, and address restrictions where possible, so that no LEASEQUERY message is sent for addresses outside the range of the attached broadband access networks. Together these mechanisms limit the access concentrator to transmitting one LEASEQUERY message, excluding message retries, per legitimate broadband access network address after a reboot event.

Packet-flooding denial-of-service attacks can exhaust processing resources and prevent the server from serving legitimate clients and legitimate leasequery requestors. While such attacks are unlikely when only trusted requestors are involved, the trust may be misplaced, security techniques may be compromised, or trusted requestors may have bugs. Techniques for defending against packet-flooding denial of service are always a good idea, and include good perimeter security and rate limiting DHCPv6 traffic by relay agents, other network elements, or the server itself. One way to attack an access concentrator as a leasequery requestor is to establish a malicious server that provides incorrect lease or route information, thwarting source address verification and preventing correct routing. This can be minimised by using IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply tells a router where a customer is, so it has to come from a server the requestor trusts. The RFC asks for the usual DHCPv6 protections, including IPsec for an access concentrator, and for the requestor to limit how many questions it asks so that it cannot be used to flood the server.
